1.note: The implication is that an army with **horses and chariots** was a very strong army, so anyone who was fighting that army would be afraid. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and see a strong army with horses and chariots]

Here, **people** represents the army of that people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a people whose army is]
The pronoun **them** refers to the army of the people group. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [of their army]
See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10.

Here Moses is speaking of Yahweh bringing the Israelites out of Egypt as if Yahweh were raising the people up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who brought you from the land of Egypt]

2.note: Here Moses is using the word translated **And it will be** to introduce an instruction. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing instructions. Alternate translation: [And it must be]

Here, **the people** represents the army of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the soldiers]

3.q: אַל־יֵרַ֣ךְ לְבַבְ⁠כֶ֗ם אַל־תִּֽירְא֧וּ וְ⁠אַֽל־תַּחְפְּז֛וּ וְ⁠אַל־תַּֽעַרְצ֖וּ מִ⁠פְּנֵי⁠הֶֽם׃ כִּ֚י יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם הַ⁠הֹלֵ֖ךְ עִמָּ⁠כֶ֑ם לְ⁠הִלָּחֵ֥ם לָ⁠כֶ֛ם עִם־אֹיְבֵי⁠כֶ֖ם לְ⁠הוֹשִׁ֥יעַ אֶתְ⁠כֶֽם
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language to state the reason before the result, you may rearrange the order of these sentences. Combine Deuteronomy 20:3–4 into a verse bridge to keep related information together. Alternate translation: [Yahweh your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to save you. Therefore you shall not soften your hearts. You shall not fear or panic or be terrified of them]

The priest is using **Israel** to represent all the fighting men of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [soldiers of Israel]

The speaker is using **soften your hearts** as a common expression of his culture to mean “be afraid.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have this meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You shall not be afraid]

The terms **fear or panic or be terrified** mean similar things. Moses is using these three terms together to emphasize how important it is for the Israelites to be brave when facing their enemies in battle. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express this emphasis with fewer words. Alternate translation: [You shall not be afraid in any way] or [You shall not let fear overcome you]

4.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since]

5.q: וְ⁠דִבְּר֣וּ הַ⁠שֹּֽׁטְרִים֮ אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם לֵ⁠אמֹר֒ מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּנָ֤ה בַֽיִת־חָדָשׁ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א חֲנָכ֔⁠וֹ יֵלֵ֖ךְ
5.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this quotation in such a way that there is not a quotation within a quotation. This quote continues until the end of verse seven. Alternate translation: [And the officers shall ask the people if there is any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it. They shall tell him to go]

5.q: מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּנָ֤ה בַֽיִת־חָדָשׁ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א חֲנָכ֔⁠וֹ יֵלֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֣ב לְ⁠בֵית֑⁠וֹ
5.note: Moses is using a question form followed by an instruction phrase in verses 5–8 for listing those exempted from military service. This pattern creates a formal, rhythmic structure in these military instructions. If your language would not use a pattern of phrases in this way, you could express these as statements rather than questions. Alternate translation: [Any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it should go and return to his house] or [If a man has built a new house and has not dedicated it, he must return home]
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

Here, **the man** represents men in general, not a specific man. Moses is referring to any Israelite soldier who fits this description. The same pattern occurs in verses 6–8 with other categories of men who may return home. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Is there any man]

The expression **dedicated it** refers to an ancient Israelite practice of ceremonially setting apart a new house, likely through a religious ceremony asking for God’s blessing before moving in. (Nothing more is known about this than appears in this text.) Moses assumes his audience would understand this cultural practice. If this information is not clear to your readers, you could make it more explicit. Alternate translation: [and has not dedicated it in a special ceremony] or [and has not formally celebrated its completion with a ceremony]

Moses is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [otherwise, he may die in battle and another man will dedicate it]

6.q: וּ⁠מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־נָטַ֥ע כֶּ֨רֶם֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א חִלְּל֔⁠וֹ יֵלֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֣ב לְ⁠בֵית֑⁠וֹ
6.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate the question as a statement or as an exclamation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Any man who has planted a vineyard and has not put it into use should go and return to his house] or [If a man has planted a vineyard and has not put it into use, he must return home]

6.q: וּ⁠מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־נָטַ֥ע כֶּ֨רֶם֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א חִלְּל֔⁠וֹ יֵלֵ֖ךְ
6.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [And if there is any man who has planted a vineyard and has not put it into use, let him go]

If you decided in the previous verse to translate **the man** in a way that represents men in general, not a specific man, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Is there any man] or [Is there anyone among you]
See how you translated “lest” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [otherwise he may die]

7.q: וּ⁠מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־אֵרַ֤שׂ אִשָּׁה֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א לְקָחָ֔⁠הּ יֵלֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֣ב לְ⁠בֵית֑⁠וֹ
7.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate the question as a statement or as an exclamation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Any man who is engaged to a woman and has not taken her should go and return to his house] or [If a man is engaged to a woman and has not taken her, he must return home]

7.q: וּ⁠מִֽי־הָ⁠אִ֞ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־אֵרַ֤שׂ אִשָּׁה֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א לְקָחָ֔⁠הּ יֵלֵ֖ךְ
7.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [And if there is any man who is engaged to a woman and has not taken her, let him go]
See how you translated the phrase “who is the man” in the previous verse.

Moses is referring to marriage and the consummation of marriage in a polite way by using the phrase **has not taken her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and has not yet married her] or [and has not completed the marriage with her]
See how you translated “lest” in the two previous verses. Alternate translation: [otherwise he may die]

8.q: וְ⁠יָסְפ֣וּ הַ⁠שֹּׁטְרִים֮ לְ⁠דַבֵּ֣ר אֶל־הָ⁠עָם֒ וְ⁠אָמְר֗וּ מִי־הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠יָּרֵא֙ וְ⁠רַ֣ךְ הַ⁠לֵּבָ֔ב יֵלֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֣ב לְ⁠בֵית֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִמַּ֛ס אֶת־לְבַ֥ב אֶחָ֖י⁠ו כִּ⁠לְבָבֽ⁠וֹ
8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And the officers shall continue to ask the people if there is any man who fears and is soft of heart. They shall tell him to go and return to his house, and the heart of his brother will not melt like his heart]

The term **and say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

8.q: מִי־הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ הַ⁠יָּרֵא֙ וְ⁠רַ֣ךְ הַ⁠לֵּבָ֔ב יֵלֵ֖ךְ וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֣ב לְ⁠בֵית֑⁠וֹ
8.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate the question as a statement or as an exclamation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Any man who fears and is soft of heart should go and return to his house] or [If a man fears and is soft of heart, he must return home]
See how you translated this phrase in the previous verse.

The terms **fears** and **is soft of heart** mean similar things. Moses is using these two terms together to emphasize the idea of a soldier lacking courage in battle. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express this emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [who is too frightened to fight bravely] or [who lacks courage for battle]

The speakers are using **melt … his heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “become afraid.” The image of a melting heart portrays courage dissolving into fear. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that he will not make his fellow soldiers lose their courage as well] or [to prevent his fear from spreading to the other soldiers]

9.q: כְּ⁠כַלֹּ֥ת הַ⁠שֹּׁטְרִ֖ים לְ⁠דַבֵּ֣ר אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֑ם וּ⁠פָֽקְד֛וּ שָׂרֵ֥י צְבָא֖וֹת בְּ⁠רֹ֥אשׁ הָ⁠עָֽם
9.note: The phrase **as the officers finish speaking to the people, then they shall appoint leaders** shows a sequence of events with one action following the other. The word “then” indicates that the appointment of leaders happens after the officers finish their speech. If your language has a different way to show this sequence of events, you can use that in your translation. Alternate translation: [after the officers finish speaking to the people, they shall appoint leaders of the armies as heads of the people] or [the officers will first finish speaking to the people and afterward they will appoint leaders of the armies as heads of the people]

Here Moses is speaking as if the military leaders were actually the **heads** of the people. Just as the head controls and directs the body, these leaders would command and direct the people in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [leaders who will command the people] or [those who will have authority over the soldiers]

10.q: כִּֽי־תִקְרַ֣ב אֶל־עִ֔יר לְ⁠הִלָּחֵ֖ם עָלֶ֑י⁠הָ וְ⁠קָרָ֥אתָ אֵלֶ֖י⁠הָ לְ⁠שָׁלֽוֹם
10.note: Here, **city** and **it** represent the people living in the city. Moses is using the place to refer to its inhabitants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Verses 11–13 continue to refer to the inhabitants in this way. Alternate translation: [When you approach a city to attack the people who live there, first offer them terms of peace] or [When you draw near to a city to fight against its inhabitants, then you shall call to them offering peace]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to surrender peacefully] or [to agree to peaceful terms]

11.note: Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The word **Peace** is a short response that means the city agrees to surrender peacefully. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [We agree to peace] or [We will surrender peacefully]

The single word **Peace** represents the city’s entire response to Israel’s offer. Different languages indicate direct speech in different ways. In your translation, use the punctuation and quotation indicators that are natural for representing this brief response in your language. Alternate translation: [“We accept your peace terms,”] or [that they agree to peace]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. It is implied that the city opens its gates to allow the Israelite army to enter. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and opens its gates to you] or [and allows you to enter the city]

The expression **found in it** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all the people in the city]

12.q: לֹ֤א תַשְׁלִים֙ עִמָּ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠עָשְׂתָ֥ה עִמְּ⁠ךָ֖ מִלְחָמָ֑ה
12.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **war**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [it does not surrender peacefully to you and instead fights against you] or [it does not agree to surrender to you and decides to attack you instead]

13.note: Here Moses uses the phrase **give it into your hand** as if the city were an object that Yahweh could physically place into the Israelites’ hands. The “hand” represents power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh your God will help you defeat it] or [and Yahweh your God will enable you to conquer it]

Moses is using **mouth of the sword** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to kill everyone” or “to completely destroy in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by putting them to the sword] or [by killing every one]

14.q: רַ֣ק הַ֠⁠נָּשִׁים וְ⁠הַ⁠טַּ֨ף וְ⁠הַ⁠בְּהֵמָ֜ה וְ⁠כֹל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִהְיֶ֥ה בָ⁠עִ֛יר כָּל־שְׁלָלָ֖⁠הּ
14.note: Moses lists specific items and then summarizes them as “all its spoil” to emphasize that the Israelites could take everything valuable from the conquered city. This kind of list followed by a summary term is a way to communicate completeness. You may need to structure this differently in your language to sound natural while conveying the same meaning. Alternate translation: [But all the valuable things in the city—the women, the children, the livestock, and everything else there] or [But everything that can be taken as plunder from the city, including the women, children, livestock, and all other possessions]

Moses is using **consume the spoil** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to use and enjoy the plunder taken from enemies.” This does not mean to literally eat everything, but rather to benefit from and make use of the captured goods. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and make use of the plunder of] or [and benefit from everything you have taken from]

15.note: It might seem that the expression **these nations here** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. Moses is referring to the Canaanite nations that were living in the land that the Israelites were about to enter. Your readers might not know which nations Moses means, so you may need to make this information explicit. Alternate translation: [the Canaanite nations that are living in the land that Yahweh is giving you] or [these nations that currently occupy the land]

16.note: Moses compares the land that Yahweh is giving to the Israelites to **an inheritance** that parents pass down to their children. Just as children permanently receive property from their parents, the Israelites would permanently receive the land from Yahweh. If this metaphor would be unclear in your language, you could express the meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [as your permanent possession] or [as land that will belong to you and your descendants permanently]

17.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **devote** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. The repetition emphasizes that the Israelites must completely devote, or destroy, these nations without exception. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. See how you translated “devoted” at 2:34. Alternate translation: [you must completely devote them] or [you must utterly destroy them]

18.q: לְמַ֗עַן אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא־יְלַמְּד֤וּ אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ לַ⁠עֲשׂ֔וֹת כְּ⁠כֹל֙ תּֽוֹעֲבֹתָ֔⁠ם
18.note: Here, **so that** marks **they do not teach you to do like any of their abominations** as the goal or purpose of the command to destroy these nations in the previous verse. Moses is explaining that the Israelites must destroy these nations to prevent them from teaching the Israelites to worship false gods. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to prevent them from teaching you to do the detestable things] or [to make sure they cannot teach you to imitate their disgusting practices]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Moses explains that the reason the Israelites should not learn the practices of these nations is that doing so would be sinning against Yahweh. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because doing these things would be sinning against Yahweh your God] or [which would cause you to sin against Yahweh your God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [their detestable practices] or [their rituals that God hates]

19.note: Here, **to capture it** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of **battling against it**. Moses describes the purpose of the military actions against the city. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [battling against it in order to capture it] or [fighting against it with the goal of taking it]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Moses gives the reason why the Israelites should not destroy the trees during a siege—because these trees provide food. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because you shall eat from them] or [since they will provide food for you]

19.q: כִּ֤י הָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ עֵ֣ץ הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֔ה לָ⁠בֹ֥א מִ⁠פָּנֶ֖י⁠ךָ בַּ⁠מָּצֽוֹר
19.note: Moses is using the question form to emphasize that trees are not human enemies who can attack the Israelites. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement. Alternate translation: [For the tree of the field is not a man who can fight against you.] or [Remember, the trees in the field are not people who can attack you.]

Moses is using **from your face** as a common expression of his culture to mean “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to come on account of the siege]

20.note: The terms **destroy it** and **cut down** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis to make clear that the Israelites may completely remove non-food trees. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [completely cut it down] or [chop it down for your use]

Here, **the city** and **it** represent the people who are actually fighting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the city where people are fighting against you] or [the city whose inhabitants are at war with you]

Moses is using the term **falls** to mean “surrenders” or “is captured.” The city is described as falling when its defenses are overcome. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until you capture the city] or [until the city surrenders to you]
